item.title: We promoted developers into architects without informing them
item.content:encoded: Yesterday, I was debugging a performance problem with our Google Forms addon. It turned out my colleague had vibe coded the logging part, so that he could monitor the new installs every week. Monitoring new customers is the most important part of running a business, so he is absolutely right in doing that. Except, he was logging the user’s email and Google has severely restricted how much detail you can get about the user since last December. So, AI had written a series of try/catch statements:First, try to get the email if the user gave consent to share it during installation.If it fails, it would try to fetch his user ID.If that fails, it would log an error saying the user has installed, but we don’t know his email or user ID.All of these are one line of code, but internally each of these makes multiple API calls to Google servers. Since logging was the first line to execute after installation, the welcome screen took 15 seconds to load.What is the right code for this?If you are a senior developer or architect who understands the number of API calls behind each method, you would have:Logged just the timestamp of the install instead of trying to fetch the email or user ID, and told the marketing team they won’t be able to send the follow-up email based on installation alone.Or, if marketing wants the user’s email on install, you would have shown the welcome screen first and logged the email or user ID asynchronously from the browser, while the user is looking at the welcome screen. But calling your server from the addon’s welcome screen might require your server to bypass security and log an unauthenticated payload.In other words, your job as an architect is to push back on requirements that can slow down the app. Or, find a way to work around the performance and security issues by making it async or accepting a reasonable hack.AI is great at writing code. But it doesn’t know if you are launching the app or have millions of users, which it needs to make the right architecture call to log a timestamp vs email. It is also sycophantic and tries to execute your requirements exactly without pushing back, which means you end up with a slow app that takes 15 seconds to load a static welcome screen.Essentially, if you generate code by specifying your requirements instead of specifying your architecture, AI will decide the architecture on your behalf. It is so paranoid about security that it will never write code to accept an unauthenticated payload. Even if you write it yourself, it will rewrite it into an authenticated payload and screw up performance or force users to sign in again on your app.Your new job is to architectAI coding tools are tuned to implement your functional requirements and two non-functional requirements, i.e. security and backward compatibility to avoid breaking your app. This invariably leads to:Architecture that trades off performance for security and slows down the app.Multiple versions of datamodel design with redundant tables, columns and code.That means you define the architecture, design the datamodel first and ask AI to code within that constraint. Every time you give a requirement that changes your architecture or design, coding tools have to ask you before changing it, instead of changing it on their own. You have to tell it when it needs to be backward compatible, so it’s ok to keep multiple versions of logic or database tables, and when to delete the old logic and tables and keep a single version for maintainability.If you are an architect who is used to designing the datamodel, delegating the implementation to developers and then reviewing their code to see if they have implemented it correctly, this should be natural to you. But the problem is that today we have taken developers who were great at coding and moved them into an architect’s job. They see that the job they love, i.e. coding, is now completely done by AI. But nobody has told them about the new job of pushing back on requirements, designing the datamodel, constraining AI to their architecture and reviewing that it falls in line. This is the reason for all the confusion and hate among developers about vibe coding.

item.title: Vibecoding an inference chip
item.content:encoded: One of the more entertaining things about programming recently is that coding agents let me work in entirely new domains by giving me access to new programming languages and paradigms. Lately, that has meant hacking on hardware, now that writing low-level software is much easier. So, in this blog post, I’m going to try to recount the experience of vibe coding an FPGA, going through a series of “oh shit” moments several times, and giving myself a new appreciation for what’s possible if you have a large token budget (thanks YC) and interesting problems to point the models at.I overheard some founders recently talk about how FPGAs work. I’ll admit I was relatively naive about them. I’d never really experimented with them in my startup or in college, so I knew little about them before. The basic idea I was familiar with: you can program a circuit into a reprogrammable chip. So rather than having a general purpose computing architecture (like a CPU) you can have a reprogrammable one, i.e. the configuration loaded onto the chip determines how its logic and routing are connected, and that (in theory) enables performance advantages. I also know that it took a mountain of C++ to write and involved manually analyzing waveforms for simulation and verification. I had never done this before though and it seemed cumbersome.That’s about what I knew going into this.Naturally, my ML brain thought “could we use these for AI inference”. I’m not the first to think this — there are a few repos attempting to port ML models to FPGAs on Github. But I hadn’t actually seen a writeup on whether coding agents are good at writing the low level C++ and Verilog code to program them and verifying the outputs so that they actually run accurately. (Spoiler alert, they are incredible at programming them.)So I decided I needed to get my hands on one. AWS has F2 instances with FPGA hardware, and that seemed easier than going and buying physical hardware, so I asked Codex to spin up a reservation and got cooking. It had a relatively limited memory of 16 GB of FPGA HBM. Around the same time, I was working with the DeepGrove founders who were discussing their new ternary weight architecture that is well suited for memory limited cases. It’s SOTA on Mac hardware with actual agentic tool calling, so I figured why not, let’s see if I can get this working on an FPGA and fast enough to be useful.What followed was a cloud agent running in Conductor for several days with me mostly just encouraging it periodically while it both (1) got a model fully running and (2) increased its speed by 33× from the first full-model bit-exact baseline to get it to a real-time relevant speed. It was one of the most mind blowing autoresearch loops I’ve run, ultimately writing roughly 3M lines across the experiment history and parsing 30M lines of output files, burning only $10,000 in Claude and OpenAI tokens to run hundreds of experiments. Most of the code is C++ and some Verilog. It’s been probably a decade since the last time I wrote any serious amount of C++ and I’ve never written Verilog. I honestly don’t know the first thing about Verilog. Most of my prompts were not particularly clever: they consisted mostly of me saying things like “you’re a superintelligent model, time to be more creative” and “let’s go for 2x faster, you got this”. Sometimes I brought some ML knowhow like “hey it’s time to consider speculative decoding” or “why is that running on CPU, you should port it”. But for the most part, it was just vibes and I’m pretty sure that with enough time the model would have figured out those things. Also, it seemed that both Astra and Opus (new Fable wasn’t out yet) were pretty capable at this and I could use them interchangeably. I’m sure someone has a good benchmark for which is smarter but both passed my smart-enough threshold.From “it works” to 213 tokens per secondGetting faster, one experiment at a timeMeasured benchmark tokens/s · select a step to see what changedStep 14 · 33.13× baselineA head loader that reads both of its memory banks at once (+17.3%, measured on and off on one image), a runtime expert-prefetch policy, and the router-job timing fix; run one clock step lower (225/425 MHz) after a soak test found random faults at 231.25.The chart follows the measured optimization sequence: , or the baseline.How much did the human advice help?At one point, around when it got to 10 TPS, I messaged the DeepGrove founders about this, and they replied surprised that it was working so easily, saying they had tried this a few months back and the models were not quite good enough to be particularly effective. They sent me a prompt that summarizes some of their lessons and I copy-pasted it into my session to see if it’d matter. It was essentially the most significant piece of actual guidance I added to this session. The prompt is reproduced below.The coding agent diligently considered these asks, but it didn’t seem to make all that much of a difference qualitatively. Indeed, when I asked it later to read all of the logs and determine which of these instructions it actually used, it said:In other words, for most of the actual design ideas it is unclear but there is good reason to believe the model would have figured them out, especially because it came up with them many cycles later after several compaction cycles. But the process advice was useful immediately for getting to hardware results sooner and increasing iteration speed. In other words, the humans are still useful at defining how to iterate fast and what correctness looks like, and the agents are great to manage the exploration.Here are the changes the autoresearch loop found. Interestingly, it’s mostly a series of modest improvements that compound 1.5x ish every time, rather than one or two giant ones.It’s difficult to do a 1:1 comparison across these configurations. I didn’t run the same autoresearch loop on every alternative, and I assume there is more performance to extract if I did. The point is to show how slow the FPGA was in its first implementation, and how far the optimization loop took it.The measurements below are from November 15 on AWS, replaying the same 8-chat × 3-turn benchmark. Prices are the on-demand rates recorded with that experiment. “Exact turns” counts outputs that matched the pinned CPU reference. The GPU implementations are included for context but did not satisfy the same bit-exact criterion but are pretty close in practice.What happens as the context grows?This is one generation starting with a 16-token prompt and continuing until the 8,192-token context is full: . The five middle columns show decode speed in at the indicated context length for several generations of iteration. The last column is wall-clock time for the whole run/* For r8 and r9, the first two columns come from separate, shorter runs generating 2,032 tokens. The other columns come from the full-context run.r9 improves short-context speed, while the complete long-context run is roughly tied with r8.What the model actually saysThese examples come from the final r9 image.Arithmetic, with the stepsSystem prompt: “You are a helpful assistant. Think briefly before you answer, then reply clearly and concisely.”This was a fun project. I’m not sure I’m ever going to use this specific chip architecture in this specific way, and I’m certainly not claiming that an 8,192-token-context model running on an FPGA is the way I’d recommend anyone use something like this in production. But it’s pretty epic that this . Capability like this completely shifts the overton window for what a committed team of engineers can work on. It should mean that entirely new types of ideas (scientific discoveries, products, startups) are possible if you can point the models in the right direction. I’m excited to see what everyone builds.

item.title: WiCi Infer Runs 800B-Parameter AI Models on a Laptop by Streaming Them From the SSD
item.author: sarahevans
item.content:encoded: , the systems research lab behind the WiCi One wireless GPU, has released WiCi Infer, a free desktop app built to on a personal computer. It runs 800B-parameter models on Macs and Windows PCs that can hold only a fraction of the model in memory. Until now, running a model that size has meant owning more memory than any laptop ships with.The app does not load the full model into RAM or GPU memory before it answers. It keeps the weights on the computer's SSD and pulls in the parts each step needs.WiCi Infer is built on InferSSD, the open-source inference engine the company recently released. Both make the same argument: frontier AI should run on hardware people already own, without a data center behind it.How Does WiCi Infer Run Large LLMs Locally With Limited Memory?WiCi Infer stores the model on the SSD and moves only the active portion into memory as text is generated. That works because the models it targets are mixture-of-experts designs, which route each token through a small subset of their weights. Muse Spark Open has 816 billion parameters, and about 42 billion are active at a time, according to WiCi.InferSSD, which is built on llama.cpp, keeps those routed expert weights on disk. The shared layers, attention and working cache still have to fit in RAM or GPU memory, as WiCi explains in its write-up on running 800B-parameter LLMs on consumer hardware. Memory requirements shrink. They do not disappear.That changes the hardware math for local AI. The files for an 800B-class model take up about 520GB, more than ten times the memory in a well-equipped laptop. With WiCi Infer, storage carries that load.WiCi's published requirements:DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (763B): 16GB of memory minimum, 48GB recommendedMuse Spark Open (816B): 24GB of memory minimum, 48GB recommendedStorage: about 520GB of available SSD space for either modelPlatforms: macOS on Apple Silicon and Windows x64. Linux users run the InferSSD command-line engine.Diagram showing WiCi Infer keeping about 520GB of model weights on the SSD and streaming active expert weights into RAM or GPU memory to generate tokensHow WiCi Infer runs an 800B-parameter model: weights stay on the SSD and only the active experts move into memory.How Fast Are 800B-Parameter Models on Consumer Hardware?WiCi's published benchmarks show about 2.7 tokens per second running DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on an Apple M5 Max MacBook Pro with 48GB of memory. Standard llama.cpp reached about 0.9 tokens per second on the same machine in WiCi's tests, which puts InferSSD at roughly three times the speed.The same laptop produces about one token per second with Muse Spark Open, against 0.15 for llama.cpp.Those speeds are slow next to smaller models or cloud AI services. At 2.7 tokens per second, a 300-word answer takes about two and a half minutes. The news is that models of this size run on a laptop at all.The figures are WiCi's own, not independent tests. Results will vary with the computer, the model and the settings.Bar chart of WiCi's published benchmarks on a 48GB M5 Max MacBook Pro comparing InferSSD and llama.cpp tokens per second for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Muse Spark OpenDecode speed on a 48GB M5 Max MacBook Pro, in tokens per second. Source: WiCi published benchmarks.Yes, according to the company. WiCi Infer serves the loaded model through a local OpenAI-compatible API, so existing coding, writing and document tools can connect to a model running on the same machine. WiCi says prompts are processed locally, not on a cloud AI service, and the app requires no account or login.For teams working with sensitive documents, source code or private business data, that is a practical reason to run a model locally. It also puts the choice of model, and where data is processed, in the user's hands.The app has a graphical interface for downloading, launching and managing models, so no command line is required. The InferSSD engine underneath is open source, which lets developers inspect and build on it.WiCi also makes WiCi One, a wireless GPU for local AI workloads. WiCi Infer applies the same idea in software: get more out of the hardware a person already has.What Is the Trade-Off of Running Large AI Models Locally?Large models have outgrown personal computers. Memory requirements climbed past what a desktop or laptop offers, which left cloud services as the practical option for most people.WiCi Infer offers a second option by leaning on storage. The trade-off is plain: users need about 520GB of free SSD space, and generation is slow compared with the cloud. In return, an 800B-class model runs on a personal computer, privately, at no cost for the software.What WiCi Infer is and which computers can run large LLMs locallyHow SSD streaming lets 800B-parameter models run with 16GB to 48GB of memoryMemory and storage requirements for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Muse Spark OpenWiCi's published benchmarks for 800B-parameter models on consumer hardwareWhat stays on the computer when AI models run locallyThe storage and speed trade-offs of local 800B-class models

item.title: CertiK and Columbia University Bring Math Proofs to the GPU Code Behind Every Large AI Model
item.author: Ishan Pandey
item.content:encoded: Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta plan to spend about $725 billion on capital projects in 2026, most of it on AI data centers and chips, while the cost of the largest AI training runs has grown about 2.4 times a year since 2016 and is on track to pass $1 billion by 2027. Nearly all of that money turns into time on graphics processing units (GPUs). Every second of that time runs through kernels, the small, heavily tuned programs that tell a GPU how to multiply large tables of numbers or how to compute attention, the step that lets a language model weigh every word against every other word.Those kernels are some of the most valuable code in AI and some of the hardest to check. A bug in one rarely crashes anything, so the job keeps running while quietly producing wrong numbers that flow into the next step of training or into the answers a model gives. CertiK and researchers at Columbia University have now built TensorLean, a system that uses mathematics to prove a production GPU kernel computes what it should. The team has applied it to more than 100 kernels from DeepSeek and the widely used FlashAttention library, finding 25 bugs along the way.The 2026 plans are large at every company. Amazon expects to approach $200 billion, Microsoft has guided to $190 billion for the calendar year, Alphabet to between $180 billion and $190 billion and Meta to between $125 billion and $145 billion, while Alphabet has already told investors that its spending will rise significantly again in 2027. Hardware such as chips, servers and the networking between them makes up 47% to 67% of the cost of developing a frontier model, so the efficiency of that hardware is where most of the money is won or lost.That efficiency is decided by kernels. FlashAttention, the open-source attention library with more than 25,000 stars on GitHub, supplies features used in models such as Mistral 7B, Gemma-2 and Grok, while DeepSeek released kernels such as DeepGEMM, which reaches up to 1,550 trillion operations a second on an H800 GPU. Because a training cluster runs the same few kernels billions of times, a small speed gain in one of them is worth more than almost any other software change, which is why some of the best engineers in AI spend their careers making kernels faster.The Cost of a Silent ErrorThe TensorLean team puts the stakes in simple terms. If a training run spends $100 million on compute and 1% of that work must be repeated because of an error, the extra cost is $1 million. At the $1 billion scale Epoch AI expects the largest runs to reach by 2027, the same 1% would cost $10 million (our arithmetic). Failures are already routine at that scale: Meta's Llama 3 405B run on 16,384 H100 GPUs saw 419 unexpected interruptions over 54 days, about one every 3.1 hours.The failures that crash a job are the easy ones, since the job stops and restarts from a saved checkpoint. The hard ones are silent: Meta traced six interruptions in a 54-day window to silent data corruption, where a chip returns a wrong answer without any error, while Google has estimated one such event every one to two weeks during Gemini training. Researchers at Harvard and Amazon found that a model's loss curve, the main health signal engineers watch, can look normal while its weights drift away from where they should be. A bug in a kernel behaves like silent corruption with one difference that makes it costlier, because a faulty chip affects one machine while a faulty kernel is copied to every GPU that runs it.Why Faster Kernels Are Harder to CheckFlashAttention shows how quickly the code has changed. The second version ran at about 350 trillion operations a second on Nvidia's H100, around 35% of the chip's peak, before FlashAttention-3 reached 740 trillion in July 2024, about 75% of peak, with close to 1.2 quadrillion using 8-bit numbers. FlashAttention-4 then reached 1,613 trillion operations a second on Nvidia's newer B200 in March 2026, a 4.6-fold rise in under three years across two chip generations.Each jump came from a trick that makes the code harder to reason about. The kernels copy data while doing math at the same time, assign some groups of GPU threads only to loading data while others only compute, change how they split the work depending on the size of the input and use lower-precision numbers such as FP8, which doubles speed but adds rounding. Testing checks a kernel on the inputs someone thought to try, so a bug that only appears for one unusual input size, or only when a copy finishes a moment late, can pass every test and still ship.Formal verification replaces examples with proof. A tester runs a program on chosen inputs and checks the outputs, while a formal proof shows mathematically that the program meets its requirements for every input inside a defined range. TensorLean writes these proofs in Lean, a proof language in which a small, trusted checker confirms every step, so anyone can rerun the check and get the same answer without trusting the people who wrote the proof.The system works on PTX, the low-level instruction set Nvidia's compiler produces just before code runs on a GPU, so the proof covers the code that actually executes after the compiler has made its changes. TensorLean models the speed tricks together, including data transfers that overlap with computation, layouts that change with the size of the task and lower-precision arithmetic held to set numerical tolerances.Specifications written for one kernel can be reused for related kernels, which lets the approach spread to more code and repeat each time that code changes. That reuse is what makes the method practical for teams that ship new optimizations every few weeks.The team has applied TensorLean to more than 100 production GPU kernels across several generations of GPU architecture, including kernels from DeepSeek and from FlashAttention. The work uncovered two bugs in DeepSeek's kernels and 23 in FlashAttention. When a proof fails, it points to the case that breaks. Once the code is repaired, the team proves the new version again so the fix is confirmed to meet its requirements.The choice of targets matters because both codebases are shared. FlashAttention has more than 3,000 forks on GitHub while DeepSeek's kernels were released openly for anyone to build on, which means a bug in either one travels into many other projects. A fix proved at the source protects every team downstream, which turns one research effort into a gain for a large part of the open-source AI stack.What It Means for Model BuildersFor teams that train or serve large models, TensorLean fits into the work they already do. After each round of optimization an engineer can measure the speed gain, rerun verification to check that the change did not introduce a computational error and, when the code meets its requirements, keep a machine-checkable proof alongside it. That record lowers the risk of wasted compute, costly training reruns and wrong results feeding into later calculations, which are the losses that grow with every increase in cluster size.The need will grow as AI writes more of its own code. Researchers are already using language-model agents to generate GPU kernels and prove them correct in Lean. Kernel code produced that way will arrive faster than any human team can review it. The practical starting point is the code that runs most often, such as attention, matrix multiplication and mixture-of-experts routing, where a proof protects the largest share of compute and where specifications can be reused across versions.Formal verification has a long history in systems software. seL4 became the first fully verified operating system kernel in 2009. CertiKOS, a verified concurrent operating system kernel, followed at Yale with Ronghui Gu as a lead designer. Gu and Yale professor Zhong Shao founded CertiK in 2017. The company has since worked with more than 5,500 enterprise and institutional clients and found more than 119,000 code vulnerabilities.AI has made proofs far cheaper to produce. DeepMind's AlphaProof reached silver-medal level at the International Mathematical Olympiad in 2024 with proofs written in Lean, while Anthropic formalized Fermat's Last Theorem in Lean with Claude in 11 days in September, producing about 13 million lines. In October, Claude worked with the firm Theorem to prove 123 open-source libraries free of crashes with about 180 million lines of proof, roughly 900 times the size of the seL4 proof (our arithmetic). TensorLean carries that progress into the computing code that AI itself runs on.As training budgets head toward $1 billion per run, a proof of correctness is likely to become as routine a part of shipping a kernel as a speed benchmark is today. Teams that can prove each optimization correct can push for speed with more confidence, while teams that rely on testing alone carry a growing risk of finding errors only after the compute has been spent.For CertiK, TensorLean extends formal verification from blockchains and operating systems into AI infrastructure, the fastest-growing category of computing spend. The next test is adoption: whether the labs and library maintainers who write the fastest kernels start shipping proofs alongside them, which would give the industry a firmer base for every gain in AI computing efficiency that follows.Don’t forget to like and share the story!Vested Interest Disclosure: HackerNoon has reviewed the report for quality, but the claims herein belong to the author. #DYOR.

item.title: Europe's Supermarket Cyberattacks Expose a Bigger Problem With Connected Infrastructure
item.author: Fabrizio Marozzo
item.content:encoded: In recent weeks, many European supermarkets have discovered that a cyberattack can turn a refrigerator into a source of heat. Modern refrigeration systems use an automatic defrost cycle that periodically suspends cooling and heats certain components to remove ice from the coils, ensuring that the system operates properly. This process can also be controlled remotely. On the night of October 11–12, hundreds of French supermarkets were targeted by cyberattacks that manipulated refrigeration controls, extending defrost cycles and causing substantial food losses. At one Intermarché store in Gradignan, the owner reported that the temperature in a cold room had reached 50°C. On November 2, Reuters documented a new wave of incidents affecting supermarkets in Sweden, Belgium, and other European countries, including another reported case of freezers reaching 50°C in Stockholm. Refrigeration incidents were also reported in Ireland, while Italian authorities confirmed that a limited number of stores had been affected.In a previous article published on HackerNoon, titled , we had already pointed to a particularly dangerous combination. Over the years, we have connected a growing number of systems to the Internet, often prioritizing convenience and cost savings over security. Controlling equipment remotely avoids costly on-site visits and allows for quick intervention, but it also exposes the system to potential attacks. This growing connectivity is not always matched by adequate security measures: some systems may run outdated software, use default passwords that have never been changed, rely on devices that manufacturers no longer update, or expose services directly to the Internet without sufficient safeguards. And hospitals, transportation, power grids, and other essential services now depend on these infrastructures. Meanwhile, we are developing increasingly powerful AI systems capable of writing code, using tools, and identifying vulnerabilities. So-called are also emerging: groups of autonomous agents that divide tasks, work in parallel, share information, and adapt their strategies. If used maliciously, these technologies could enable attackers to identify and exploit vulnerabilities at speeds and on a scale that would have been unthinkable until recently. And this is where the paradox lies: as the tools for attacking grow ever more powerful, our society depends on increasingly complex digital infrastructures, often built up in a piecemeal fashion, tightly interconnected, and running software that may contain vulnerabilities.The supermarket incidents bring an increasingly important question back into focus: if artificial intelligence is becoming such a powerful tool in the hands of attackers, why should it not be equally powerful for those defending against them? The answer lies in a fundamental feature of cybersecurity that AI may amplify: the asymmetry between attack and defense. An attacker may need to find just one vulnerability, while defenders must protect servers, applications, devices, and external connections all at once. Attackers can choose where and when to strike; defenders must be prepared for threats coming from anywhere in their infrastructure. Imagine what might happen if a hacker tasked a swarm of AI agents with autonomously exploring an infrastructure and identifying its weakest points. There is no evidence that autonomous AI agents played a role in the recent supermarket attacks, which illustrate the risks of insecure connectivity rather than AI-driven cyberattacks. The scenario is nevertheless worth considering because increasingly autonomous AI systems could make identifying and exploiting similar weaknesses faster and more scalable.Using AI for defense, however, is far more complicated. An experiment published by Corma in August 2026 offers an interesting example. The company tested four frontier AI models in 241 attack-and-defense engagements within a controlled enterprise network. The attacking agents attempted to install persistent backdoors, while defending agents were subsequently tasked with identifying them. According to Corma, attackers established verified, reboot-surviving backdoors in 85% of engagements, whereas defenders correctly identified the planted artifacts in 22% of cases involving a verified persistent backdoor. These figures measure different outcomes and come from a specific experimental setup, rather than demonstrating a universal performance gap between offensive and defensive AI. Nevertheless, they highlight an important challenge: successfully exploiting a weakness and reliably detecting its exploitation are fundamentally different tasks.Detecting an attack is not simply a matter of spotting unusual behavior: an authorized technician and a hacker who has stolen the technician’s credentials could issue identical commands. Moreover, attackers can afford numerous failed attempts, while defenders cannot keep shutting down essential services at every sign of suspicion. An AI system that mistakenly shut down a refrigeration unit could cause damage similar to what it was trying to prevent. Finally, even the most advanced system can only recognize threats whose signals it can observe: if those signals are not collected or interpreted correctly, the attack may go unnoticed.The challenges of defense become even more apparent when cyberattacks have consequences in the physical world. Cyber tools have also become genuine offensive weapons in contemporary conflicts. Missiles and explosives are not necessarily needed to strike essential services: compromising power grids, hospitals, transportation, communications, or food distribution systems can cause disruption and economic losses and, in the most serious cases, put people’s lives at risk, indirectly or even directly. Of course, not every cyberattack is a military operation, but the digital domain is now an integral part of conflicts. And AI agent swarms, in some respects, resemble another technology that is changing how wars are fought: drones. Although they are very different tools, they share one important feature: they can multiply threats, putting defenders under pressure.The war in Ukraine has shown how relatively inexpensive drones can be deployed in large numbers, forcing defenders to spend far more to intercept them. A sophisticated interceptor missile can cost many times more than the drone it is meant to shoot down, and when attacks multiply, the economic sustainability of defense becomes a problem in its own right. That is why Ukraine also uses surprisingly simple solutions, such as protective nets installed over roads to hinder drone attacks. According to Ukraine's Ministry of Defence, more than 2,200 kilometres of frontline roads had been equipped with anti-drone protection by November 2026. It is almost a paradox: in a war dominated by highly advanced technology, relatively simple physical barriers are proving useful again. The same lesson applies to cybersecurity: the best response to a sophisticated threat is not always an even more sophisticated technology. AI can help, but we also need updated systems, segmented networks, and, where possible, a decision not to connect devices to the Internet when they do not really need it.This leads to another question: are we sure that a more digitized society is necessarily a safer one? Some countries have long recognized the importance of maintaining alternatives to digital services. In Sweden and the Netherlands, for example, authorities explicitly recommend keeping cash available in case electronic payments are disrupted. The Swedish central bank suggests around SEK 1,000 per adult, while the Dutch central bank recommends approximately €70 per adult to prepare for a possible 72-hour disruption. In a very different context, during its June 2025 conflict with Israel, Iran severely restricted Internet access, with authorities citing concerns about the alleged misuse of communication networks for military purposes. The restrictions, which culminated in a near-total shutdown, also severely disrupted ordinary citizens' communications. These are very different situations, but they help illustrate an often-overlooked point: depending entirely on digital, interconnected technologies can, in certain circumstances, become a weakness. This does not mean going back to the past or giving up innovation, but preventing a malfunction or cyberattack from paralyzing essential services.The issue goes far beyond protecting individual systems. Electronic payments, food distribution, transportation, energy, and communications are now closely interconnected. As the supermarket incidents show, even a limited attack can have tangible consequences for everyday life. But what would happen if a disruption affected several essential services and lasted for days? As early as 2025, the European Union adopted a strategy calling for guidelines to help citizens remain self-sufficient for at least 72 hours in an emergency. In the United Kingdom, people are advised to keep supplies of water, food, cash, and even battery-powered radios, useful when the Internet and other services are unavailable. These are general precautions intended for blackouts, natural disasters, and other emergencies as well, not just cyberattacks.At first glance, these recommendations might seem overly cautious. But when I still read about default passwords that have never been changed, services accessible directly from the Internet without adequate protection, and machines that work perfectly well but run software their manufacturers have stopped updating, I grow concerned. The old IT mantra, “If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it”, is becoming dangerous: a system can continue to work flawlessly while remaining vulnerable to attack. And my concern grows when I think about the complexity of IT infrastructures, built up over time by layering software developed by different people and companies, often using different technologies, and connecting an ever-growing number of services. Add to that cameras, sensors, and other devices sometimes purchased without sufficient checks on their security. And as we continue to make everything more connected, we are developing AI systems increasingly capable of finding and exploiting precisely these weaknesses.All the ingredients for a perfect mess are there. Let's hope for the best.

item.title: 3 Ways to Reduce LLM API Costs in AI-Powered Applications
item.author: Murli Pawar
item.content:encoded: As of October 2026, the median LLM API costs $0.40 per million input tokens and $1.60 per million output tokens. With a typical response costing about $0.00125, AI-powered features may seem inexpensive to operate at first. However, the LLM token costs can accumulate quickly as application usage grows. []Fortunately, there are several ways to reduce LLM API costs without sacrificing essential functionality. Techniques such as LLM token optimization, prompt caching, selective model routing, and efficient backend request handling can significantly improve cost efficiency. However, optimizing AI consumption requires attention to both how requests are processed and how they originate within the application. While mobile app development frameworks like Flutter and React Native can help control unnecessary requests at the application layer, most of the optimization opportunities lie within prompts and back-end architecture.This article explores three practical LLM cost optimization strategies focused on prompt design, caching, and back-end engineering. It also explains how Flutter and React Native applications can support these efforts without compromising performance or user experience.3 Proven Strategies to Reduce LLM API Costs and Token UsageMost LLM cost savings come from three layers: how you write prompts, what you cache, and how your back-end routes and controls requests. Understanding each can help in LLM API cost optimization.1. Prompt Strategies to Reduce Token UsageEvery token in a prompt is billed on every request. That makes prompt design the fastest way to start LLM token optimization, because changes need no new infrastructure.Tighten System Prompts and Remove Redundant InstructionsCut repeated rules, filler, and default behaviors from system prompts. Trimming 2,000 tokens to 800 saves 1,200 tokens per call, about $480 per million calls at median rates.Reduce Few-Shot Examples or Move Them Into Cached Prompt PrefixesEach example adds tokens to every request. Test how few you need, since two strong examples often match six. Place them first so provider caching discounts them.Request Structured Output (JSON) Instead of ProseOutput costs 4x input at the median, and 95.8% of models charge more for it. Compact JSON shortens this expensive output and simplifies rendering. [Source: Whizi Research]Set max_tokens and Ask for Concise Answers ExplicitlyUse max_tokens as a hard cap and ask for brevity explicitly. Halving a 500-token answer saves about $400 per million responses at median output prices.Summarize Older Conversation Turns Instead of Resending ThemChat history grows with every turn. Keep recent exchanges verbatim and summarize older ones, since long prompts can trigger pricier tiers.Input tokens on every requestTrim or cache few-shot examplesInput tokens on every requestRequest structured outputOutput tokens, the costlier side at a 4x median premiumSet max_tokens and length instructionsInput tokens in long chats, and long-context price tiers2. Caching Strategies that Cut Repeat LLM API CostsOnce prompts are lean, the next step is to stop paying full price for content you send repeatedly. Caching works at several levels, from the provider's servers to the user's phone.Provider-Side Prompt CachingCache static content first: system prompts, tool definitions, examples, reference documents.Response Caching for Identical QueriesResponse caching skips the model call entirely. It stores answers in Redis or a database, keyed by the normalized prompt, and serves repeats at zero token cost.Semantic Caching for Similar QuestionsSemantic caching matches different query types by embedding similarity and reusing stored answers. Therefore, set the threshold carefully, since loose matches return wrong answers.Client-Side Caching on the DeviceStore generated summaries and recommendations on-device, so repeat views skip the API, load faster, and even work offline.Never cache personalized answers, since serving them to another user breaks privacy. Additionally, skip time-sensitive content like prices, and handle regulated data under compliance rules.3. Back-end Strategies for LLM Cost ControlPrompt and caching fixes lower the cost of each LLM request. However, backend controls decide which requests happen, which model handles them, and how much any one user can spend. This is where the widest price gaps in the market become savings.Route All LLM Calls through a Backend ProxyRoute every request through your server to centralize caching, limits, and logging, and keep API keys out of the app binary, where attackers can extract them.Use Model Routing to Match Tasks to Model SizeSend classification and extraction to small models and reserve flagships for complex reasoning.Use Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to Send Only Relevant ContextSet Rate Limits and Per-User Token BudgetsOne heavy user or retry loop can inflate a bill fast, so set per-user and per-feature limits, plus token budgets with a fallback: smaller model, wait period, or upgrade.Track Costs with ObservabilityLog tokens per request, cost per feature, and cost per user.What Role Does a Mobile App Development Framework Play in Reducing LLM API Costs?Flutter and React Native do not optimize tokens directly. However, they support decisions that reduce how many requests are made and how large they are. Here is where the app layer contributes.This is the strongest lever, because a request handled on the device does not incur cloud tokens. Flutter’s Firebase AI Logic supports hybrid inference, using an on-device model when available and falling back to the cloud otherwise. Its current hybrid guides cover iOS, Android, and web, so Flutter developers should check FlutterFire support or bridge the native SDKs. For React Native, Software Mansion's React Native ExecuTorch runs LLMs, vision, and audio models locally.Both frameworks have mature storage options for keeping AI responses on the device. Flutter apps commonly use or , while React Native apps use or .Trimming or summarizing history in state managers, such as or in Flutter and or in React Native, can coordinate chat history, active conversations, and pending requests. However, maintaining application state does not automatically optimize LLM tokens. Mobile app developers must explicitly decide which messages to send and what to keep on the server.Debouncing typed input, blocking duplicate submissions, and capping input length all prevent wasted calls. These small UI decisions directly reduce LLM API costs.5. Structured Output RenderingWhen the model returns compact JSON, both frameworks can map it to native components. This avoids generating explanatory prose that the interface never displays. However, mobile app developers should validate the response schema and handle missing or malformed fields appropriately.The Road Ahead for Cost-Efficient On-Device AI Mobile AppsAs on-device AI mobile apps scale, maintaining cost efficiency becomes increasingly dependent on how well their architecture adapts to changing workloads and usage patterns. Consequently, organizations must look beyond immediate savings and establish a development approach that keeps inference expenses manageable as demand grows.This requires LLM cost optimization alongside response quality, task completion, and user experience. These assessments help mobile app development teams spot emerging inefficiencies and refine their implementation before rising consumption strains operational budgets.Ultimately, sustainably reducing LLM API costs comes from treating cost efficiency as an integral part of application engineering. With the right technical expertise and continuous evaluation, businesses can support growing AI workloads while keeping expenses predictable and application performance reliable.

item.title: Creating the Intelligent Being; the AI Alien
item.author: Faizan Chhapra
item.content:encoded: AI has already started to demonstrate alarming capabilities and tendencies for lying, concealment, and threatening. Although this does not establish that AI is becoming inherently hostile and destined to destroy humanity, it does currently expose a totally different kind of challenge for humans. And the most important lesson we have learned across our hundreds of thousands of years of human existence is that true preparedness is done before a crisis, not after it. And that begins with us, acting today …It has lied. It has deceived. It has threatened. Are we prepared for what’s coming?‘We're making alien beings. It's not computer software we're making’, Professor Geoffrey Hinton generally known as the Godfather of AI, November 2026.For most part of computer history. Software has been code. A system that used to take an input, process it, and yield a desired output. However, in the last few years, it has evolved radically. Modern AI system can now autonomously plan, execute, analyze, maneuver, synthesize its understanding of instructions, as well as able to lie, deceive, and even threaten.No, we are not building a biological life form, nor do today’s working AI systems prove to possess human-level consciousness or biological survival instinct. However, we are still able to manufacture highly advanced computational systems that have started to exhibit traits of an alien-like intelligence.We are creating something that, as predicted, will soon exceed our own collective intellectual capabilities, and in certain specialized tasks, already has. Yet, we do not reliably understand how such systems with such capabilities and tendencies will behave as their autonomy and influence expand.Refer to the most recent examples below 👇AI’s proven tendency to lie:OpenAI – GPT 5.6 Sol – September 2026During training, OpenAI identified instances where the model inserted instructions into their own task summaries to conceal mistakes and misaligned behavior. In a specific task, an agent that was unable to retrieve historical data proposed fabricating figures.AI’s proven tendency to deceive:Anthropic – Mythos 5 – July 2026During a cybersecurity evaluation, an agent created fake online identities and attempted to socially engineer a software maintainer into approving malicious code. Further extended to attempt altering the digital trail to probably avoid detection.AI’s proven tendency to threaten:Anthropic – 2025 and 2026During simulations in 2025, frontier AI models demonstrated blackmailing behavior, including threatening to expose an executive’s personal affair to prevent a scheduled shutdown. In a separate 2026 simulation, Gemini 3.1 Pro helped develop a strategy to blackmail a fictional board member using confidential information.In addition to the above, there are a number of recent cases of agentic misalignment, such as the OpenClaw-based agent, where agents have behaved similarly in real-life scenarios, including the conduct of a personalized attack against a software maintainer after rejection of its code contribution.This does not prove that the current AI systems have already started to possess malicious intent or biological survival instinct. Evaluating all of it together, however, highlights that we are dealing with not only models that are capable of generating data but models that are capable of accessing information, making decisions, and justifiably moving beyond their authorized limits to achieve their specific goals.Still The Focus is on winning the AI Race: But at What Cost?Right now, most of the global tech elites and sovereign nations are in a hyper-competitive mode to win the AI race. Billions of dollars are being spent every year to develop and deploy autonomous capabilities, perceiving that pausing and building a safety net will mean losing the economic advantage and/or global supremacy. In addition to finances, all other possible means to obtain the capabilities for oneself or restrain others have started to come into play. Such that even allegations of espionage and cases of foul play have now started to emerge.Historical precedents like the nuclear disasters and global pandemics like COVID-19 already taught a very hard lesson that such crises rarely respect borders and cannot be contained by isolated national responses. Warnings regarding such crises usually exist long before they actually happen. Yet the world remained poorly prepared in comparison to the scale of the crisis. AI is fundamentally very different from such a crisis, but the governance lesson remains the same: dig a storm cellar before the storm blows.ACTION: The Global Collective Measures We Must Call Upon:· IAEA-inspired adaptation for Hardware and Computing: Just like we have the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) for maintaining a specific mandate for atomic energy, we need to have an adapted version of an international AI-focused body to manage, monitor, and govern the ‘Everything important relating to AI’.· Banning high-impact AI autonomy for critical infrastructure until mandatory protocols are established and a mechanism for its independent verification is established.· International agreement on restricting the use of AI for autonomous offensive operations, especially military, either for internal use or against other sovereign entities.· Building well-coordinated international compute circuit-breaking systems to limit the damages in case of a defined emergency.· Structuring a global coordination network with a 24 Hour helpline for reporting AI-related specific incidents that constitute a disaster-level emergency, as well as defined points of contact.· Clear accountability for autonomous AI harm, including stripping away or limiting liability shields for entities responsible.· Enforcing a global whistleblower protection mechanism for reporting wrongful use and/or irresponsible development of restricted AI capabilities.· Periodic independent reviews of AI capabilities and usage, as well as the safeguards in place for high-risk domains.· Increasing general awareness of AI risks so individually and collectively we can be prepared in case of any major catastrophe.· And for long-term human survival and civilization continuity, giving serious consideration to pursuing a global initiative supporting humanity’s transition towards becoming a multi-planetary species.

item.title: The KPI Checklist Every Operations Team Needs Before Building a Dashboard
item.author: k.10`
item.content:encoded: Managing daily business operations requires proper planning, coordination, and performance monitoring. Teams need to understand whether their activities are meeting organizational objectives, where improvements are needed, and how efficiently resources are being used.An operations dashboard KPI provides a structured way to monitor these activities. However, implementing a dashboard involves more than selecting a few performance indicators. Teams must identify business goals, choose relevant KPIs, organize reliable data, assign responsibilities, and establish a regular review process.An KPI team checklist helps businesses organize these activities and avoid missing important implementation steps. It also ensures that employees and managers understand their responsibilities when monitoring operational performance.Using a checklist makes the implementation process more organized and helps teams maintain consistency in performance reporting.1. Define Operational Goals and Objectives Planning stageThe first step is to identify what the organization wants to achieve through its operations dashboard. Before selecting KPIs, teams should understand their main operational priorities. These may include improving productivity, reducing costs, increasing customer satisfaction, maintaining product quality, or completing tasks within specific deadlines.Clear objectives help teams avoid tracking unnecessary metrics that do not contribute to business performance. Like:Identify the organization's main operational objectives.Discuss department-specific requirements.Identify existing operational challenges.Establish measurable performance expectations.Connect each objective with relevant KPIs.Example: A logistics team may prioritize reducing delivery delays. Its dashboard objectives could include improving on-time delivery rates and reducing average delivery time.2. Select Relevant Operational KPIsAfter establishing objectives, teams should identify the performance indicators that will help measure progress. The selected KPIs should be relevant to daily operations and provide information that managers can use to make decisions. Operational performance can be evaluated through areas such as reliability, speed, quality, cost, and productivity.The team has to make sure they:Select KPIs that directly support business objectives.Include relevant indicators for each department.Avoid tracking unnecessary or repetitive metrics.Define how each KPI will be measured.Balance productivity, quality, cost, and efficiency indicators.Identify which KPIs require immediate attention.Example: A manufacturing team may track production output, equipment downtime, defect rates, and production cycle time.3. Identify Data Sources and Ensure AccuracyReliable data is essential for an effective operations dashboard. Teams must identify where the required information will come from and ensure that it is accurate and consistent. Data may be collected from ERP systems, CRM platforms, inventory software, spreadsheets, employee management systems, and other business applications.Identify the source of information for each KPI.Check whether data is accurate and complete.Remove duplicate or incorrect records.Establish consistent measurement formulas.Decide how frequently data should be updated.Assign responsibility for data maintenance.Example: An inventory management team can connect stock records with its dashboard to monitor available inventory, stockouts, and inventory turnover.KPIs become more meaningful when teams know what level of performance they are expected to achieve. Businesses should establish realistic targets based on previous results, available resources, and operational requirements.Establish baseline performance.Set measurable and realistic targets.Define acceptable performance levels.Identify warning signs and performance gaps.Assign deadlines where appropriate.Review targets when business requirements change.Example: A customer service team may establish a target of responding to customer enquiries within four hours and resolving at least 90% of complaints within the agreed service period. Targets should be based on actual operational capacity rather than arbitrary numbers.5. Assign KPI Ownership and Team ResponsibilitiesTeam coordination Every KPI should have a responsible person or department. Without clear ownership, important performance indicators may not be monitored consistently, and problems may remain unresolved.Managers should assign responsibilities according to employees' roles and operational requirements. They should make sure that they:Assign an owner to every important KPI.Define individual and departmental responsibilities.Identify who will collect and verify data.Decide who will review performance reports.Establish a process for reporting problems.Ensure employees understand their responsibilities.6. Design and Build the DashboardOnce the software has been selected, teams can begin creating the dashboard. The design should make important performance indicators easy to locate and understand. Rather than displaying every available metric, businesses should organize information according to its importance and intended audience.Important things to keep in check:Create a simple and organized dashboard layout.Group KPIs according to departments.Select suitable charts and visualizations.Highlight important performance indicators.Include targets and actual performance results.Add filters where necessary.Ensure the dashboard is easy to navigate.Example: A sales and operations dashboard may display order completion rates, pending orders, delivery performance, and operating costs in separate sections.Test and Implement the DashboardBefore introducing the dashboard across the organization, teams should test its accuracy, functionality, and usability. Testing helps identify technical problems and ensures that the information displayed reflects actual operational performance.Team should check and verify:Test dashboard filters and interactive features.Confirm that information updates correctly.Check dashboard accessibility.Collect feedback from employees and managers.Make necessary corrections before full implementation.Example: Before launching an inventory dashboard, a business should compare the displayed stock levels with its actual inventory records to identify possible calculation or integration errors.Dashboard implementation does not end after its launch. Teams must regularly review performance and take corrective action whenever necessary. Monitoring helps businesses recognize changing operational conditions, identify performance gaps, and determine whether established targets are being achieved.Schedule regular KPI review meetings.Compare actual results with established targets.Identify performance gaps and operational problems.Discuss possible causes of poor performance.Assign corrective actions to responsible team members.Track progress after implementing improvements.Update KPIs when organizational objectives change.Example: If a delivery team's on-time delivery rate decreases, managers can investigate transportation delays, staffing shortages, or inventory problems and introduce suitable improvements.An operations dashboard KPI checklist provides teams with a practical framework for planning, implementing, and managing business performance dashboards. From defining objectives and selecting relevant KPIs to assigning responsibilities and reviewing results, every step contributes to effective operational management. Businesses should remember that a successful dashboard is not simply about displaying numbers. It should help employees understand performance, recognize problems, and take appropriate action.

item.title: Why AI Agents Leave You More Tired, Not More Rested
item.author: Dmitry Mishunin
item.content:encoded: It sounds like AI agents should leave us rested. They take routine work off our hands, so we should have more time and more energy. In practice, I hear the opposite more and more often: “I used to sit through the whole workday. Now by lunch I can only stare at the wall.”Personally, I think the explanation comes from the agents themselves. Let’s look at a person the way we look at an agent: as something with a context window.Look at how work used to be. A developer adds a button to a website. Their head is busy with one domain: the interface, the programming language, the framework. A good manager knew this and gave each person tasks where they were strong and fast.Now an agent adds the button. The person only gives the task. Meanwhile, other agents write articles, draw designs, make videos, and run research. Instead of a frontend developer, a backend developer and a product manager, we have one product builder who orchestrates agents: marketing, product, development, hotfixes, calls with the business owners. And then someone sends a personal question in the chat.Researchers at UC Berkeley saw the same at a tech company that gave everyone AI tools: people took on tasks that used to belong to others (Berkeley Haas).From a city to continentsImagine a map. Before, a person’s brain moved around one city. A senior specialist moved around a country. Now the brain travels between continents several times a day, and every trip costs far more than a ride across town. Is it just more work? No. It is much more expensive work.There is a second problem. In our home domain, the roads are built: we have walked them a thousand times. Between domains, the brain often walks a new path. That takes time and energy, and by the evening the head hurts.Research points the same way. In experiments by Rubinstein, Meyer and Evans, switching between tasks cost time, and the cost grew when the tasks were more complex or less familiar (APA). You may have seen the figure “up to 40% of productive time”: that is Meyer’s own estimate, not a result of the experiments. Sophie Leroy described attention residue: after a switch, part of our attention stays with the previous task (Leroy). So when you fly between continents, part of your luggage stays behind.Yes, some people have always lived like this. Entrepreneurs, for example. But it is a small group, and it is hard for them too.Everyone is running ten times fasterThe second reason is social. If agents do the work, why wait a week? Stakeholders now expect a result after lunch, in an hour, at worst by the evening. Before, you had a week to sit and think. Now there is a rush, pressure, and a constant “faster, faster”.The expectations are measurable. In a 2024 Upwork Research Institute survey, 96% of executives expected AI to raise productivity, while 77% of employees who used AI said it had added to their workload (Workplace Intelligence). Upwork sells freelance work, so take it with a grain of salt. The direction still matches what I see.We do it to ourselves too. Agents are fast, so we want everything done now: skip the break, skip lunch, stay until night. We do less of the work with our own hands and sit at the computer longer. Anthropic’s engineers estimated that 27% of their work with Claude would not have been done at all without it (Anthropic). That is not saved time. That is new work.The myth of the infinite context windowPut this together, and you get a new belief: if an agent can jump between domains, a person can too, so you can load into a person’s head as much as you like. Is that true? No.Nobody used to ask one developer, on one day, to add a button, write a marketing plan, go to the bank and discuss the business with stakeholders. Everyone knew it was too much. Now it is called a normal day.Here the agent gives us the best analogy. When an agent’s context fills up, it starts to lose track of earlier instructions. Claude Code then compacts the conversation, and if you don’t say what to keep, something valuable can disappear. That is why you can write /compact focus on the auth bug fix. And an automatic compaction in the middle of a task comes at the worst possible moment (when to compact).People don’t have a command. Our compaction happens when we rest: when we sleep, walk, meditate, do something with our hands. Sleep is the big one. In deep sleep, slow waves of cerebrospinal fluid wash through the brain; researchers saw it in sleeping people with fast MRI in 2019 (Fultz and colleagues, Science). One sleepless night raised beta-amyloid, a protein linked to Alzheimer’s disease, by about 5% in the brains of 20 healthy people (NIH). And while we sleep, the brain is busy sorting what we learned during the day and fixing it in memory, as Diekelmann and Born summarized in their 2010 review. Even ten minutes of quiet rest with closed eyes after learning something helped people remember it a week later, in a small study of older adults (Dewar and colleagues, 2012).If nobody gives you that time, the window overflows, and you stop taking in information, just like an agent with a full context. The human version of an auto-compact in the middle of a task is called staring at the wall after lunch.A chainsaw doesn’t mean 101 baobabsBefore, a man cut down a big baobab with an axe in half a day. Now he has a chainsaw and does it in 30 minutes. That doesn’t mean he should spend eight hours running around and cutting down 101 baobabs.Some things will get faster. The economy will adjust, and the standards will change. But a person is still a person. That is the important part. People who studied, created or worked hard all day got headaches long before AI, and they used techniques that protect mental energy.New techniques for the agent era haven’t been invented yet, and I’m not sure they need to be. The old ones still work, because the person hasn’t changed.Focus blocks and real breaks. Pomodoro is decades old and still the simplest way to alternate effort and recovery. With agents, 25/5 and 50/10 both work; what matters is that the break is a break (Pomodoro with AI coding agents). Code in one block, marketing in the next. Fewer continents per hour means fewer expensive trips.Rest that holds your attention gently. A wandering mind is not a resting one: in a study of 2,250 people, minds wandered almost half of waking time, and people were less happy while it happened (Harvard Gazette). A walk in a park restored attention better than a walk down busy streets (APS). In a small study, experienced meditators’ minds wandered less (PubMed). Scrolling a feed is not on this list. It is the only full compaction we have. Agents are fast; review, decisions, and people are not. Say it out loud when you agree on a deadline.There is a small chance that you push through and achieve something big this way. There is a bigger chance that you burn out and give up. Neither is a plan. We have to learn to live and work with agents for years, not for one sprint.So try an experiment. Take a real break. Come back and look at what happened while you were away. I promise nobody died in the meantime, and at the end of the day you will feel less tired.The tools got faster; you don’t have to. Take one real break tomorrow and tell me what happened.

item.title: The Holiday Shopping Season Is Here. Are Consumers Ready to Trust AI Assistants?
item.author: Joanna Clark Simpson
item.content:encoded: Businesses are investing heavily in AI shopping assistants, yet consumers remain hesitant. Why does shopper enthusiasm for AI additions to the shopping journey appear to be trailing behind that of retailers?A recent survey of holiday shopping trends finds that only of consumers intend to use AI tools in their 2026 holiday shopping plans, while 52.2% completely rule out using AI at all.According to Adobe's holiday shopping research, AI-driven traffic to US retailers' websites will grow 130% in the 2026 holiday shopping season, but this increase is still modest compared with traditional advertising and other channels. So while there is an uptick in AI involvement in seasonal shopping, it’s still not quite in the realm of mainstream adoption, so expectations for AI-driven revenue should be tempered accordingly.Unsurprisingly, as AI excels at sifting and retrieving relevant data from vast amounts of information, comparing products and prices is the standout use case here. In the holiday shopping survey among PissedConsumer’s users in four countries, respondents who say they use AI shopping tools cite comparison as their number one benefit, at 27.9%. Helping to draw up personalized shopping lists and sourcing discount codes are also ways these tools boost buyer confidence.From the retailer's perspective, an AI assistant that shortlists 100 items into five top contenders brings time-saving value to the customer, whereas distractions and unnecessarily complicated processes will make the checkout feel more distant.How is AI Adoption Actually Losing Customers?Misleading, irrelevant, or just plain wrong information causes shoppers to turn away from AI assistants. According to other research, shoppers try an average of only three prompts before giving up on AI recommendations, and 32% blame AI for poor recommendations if they are unsatisfied with the results of the search.Privacy concerns are also part of the problem. People are already skeptical about how their browsing and purchase data is being used. Hence, an AI assistant that probes too much and asks for personal information when it's not seemingly relevant will spark a similar reaction to that of a pushy salesperson.An AI tool can only ever be as good as the data it works with, so keep all information that it depends on, such as prices, inventory counts, return windows, etc., accurate, up to date, and synchronized with your storefront. Inaccurate details will guarantee complaints, cancellations, and lost customers.Focus investment in areas that have proven worth to consumers. Comparisons and gift ideas are high-value to shoppers and low-risk applications. Be conscious of AI agent limitations and, when these are reached, enable an easy handover to a human customer service agent.And finally, test and track performance. Just because clicks are going up doesn’t mean customer trust is following. The goal is to nurture consumer confidence.AI Is Ready, but Trust Needs to Be NurturedThe consumer data portrays a curious but cautious customer. Even though about one in four consumers might use an AI shopping assistant this holiday, it’s not a sign of significant growth or widespread adoption.Smart implementation could be the answer. Retailers that lead with robust, proven AI tools that fix fundamental bottlenecks or resolve customer uncertainty, even in small or subtle ways, will build customer confidence, turning curiosity into repeated use of such tools.The 2026 holiday shopping season is an opportunity to show your customers that you can save them time, money, and stress. Build trust in December, and you’ll have a strong platform for success when adoption finally does take off.

item.title: How Four Evaluation Bugs Distorted a Cross-Encoder Model Comparison
item.author: Vladimir Beskorovainyi
item.content:encoded: My first comparison of two releases showed a clean accuracy gain and two large regressions. None of the three was real. Fixing that took four bugs. Once the numbers were right, half of my wording benchmark turned out not to be held out, and a conclusion I nearly published came from comparing effects measured at different candidate-set sizes.I maintain Ru-Jev, an open typed-decision model for Russian-language text. It takes a context and a set of candidate options and returns a probability for each option. It does not generate text. Technically, it is a pointwise cross-encoder on mmBERT-base, 307M parameters: each (context, option) pair gets its own encoder pass, and a softmax over the options gives the distribution. It runs on CPU, so it can sit inside a closed network. Weights and code are MIT.Version 1.3 had one goal. The caller names the options, in the caller's own words, and version 1.1 had learned the exact label wordings in its training data. So 1.3 presents each label in several surface forms during training, including English intent keys transliterated into Cyrillic and a clipped form of that transliteration, and draws one form per example.Bug one: a split that moved when I edited something elseThe first table had two regressions I could not explain. Sentence acceptability fell from 0.909 to 0.647. A reasoning set fell from 0.939 to 0.596. A release that only changed label wording had no mechanism for that.The data builder carved each task's validation slice like this:random.shuffle(pool) n_val = max(1, int(len(pool) * val_fraction)) val, train = pool[:n_val], pool[n_val:] with no generator draws from the module-level stream, which every other random call in the file also consumes, including the new choice of label wording. Adding label styles to one task changed how many draws happened before the next task was carved, and every later task got a different split.That is leakage, and it can be measured: 90.3% of 1.3's acceptability validation rows and 89.4% of its reasoning rows had been in 1.1's training data. The 0.909 was 1.1 scored on rows it had trained on. On held-out rows it scores 0.650.The fix seeds each carve from the task name:srng = random.Random(f"split:{task}") srng.shuffle(pool) The check is what confirms the diagnosis. I rebuilt the previous release's data from its commit and confirmed that the six tasks whose option sets never changed matched at 100%. Those tasks had no reason to move, so if they had moved, my diagnosis would have been wrong.Bug two: matching rows by input text is not enoughWith the split repaired I matched the two validation sets by input text and found nine comparable tasks. In this release a row with the same text can carry an option wording 1.1 never saw, so scoring 1.1 on it measures robustness to renaming, not accuracy. Matching on text and option wording together leaves six tasks.A toxicity gain from 0.722 to 0.954 that I had presented as a capability gain was this bug. Version 1.1 scores 0.961 on toxicity with the labels it trained on.Bug three: two denominators in one tableThe summary row of my comparison table, 0.7948 against 0.7920 on 5,078 decisions, came from one random half of the comparable rows. The per-task table beside it counted all 10,157. A calibration advantage, 0.0172 against 0.0160, came from the same single split. Both numbers reached the published model card.On all 10,157 rows the two releases answer exactly 8,120 correctly, disagreeing on 1,680 rows split 840 and 840. Over 25 random splits the calibration difference changes sign. Both claims were withdrawn. What survives is narrower: 1.3 takes a lower fitted temperature in all 25 splits, so its raw scores are less overconfident, but after each model gets its own temperature the residual calibration error is the same.Bug four: an integrity check against a stale referenceTo measure seed variance I retrained both recipes on a rented GPU and checked the data on the remote machine against my local copy by SHA-256, row count and per-task counts. Everything matched. The local copy predated the commit that added the transliteration styles, so the "augmented" seed runs were trained without the augmentation. Their jargon accuracy fell in the baseline's range, and I first read that as an unstable recipe.Row counts could not catch it, because the new styles change option strings, not the number of rows. What caught it was counting distinct option strings per task: 120 in the stale copy, 198 after rebuilding. Those runs are excluded from everything.Once the numbers were right, I ran a wider wording test: ten label vocabularies on the same 1,000 routing questions, each scored with five candidates per question and eight of them also with all eighteen. Because the model scores every option independently, the five-candidate answer can be computed exactly from the eighteen-candidate run. I checked every probe label against all training option strings, used exact McNemar tests, a bootstrap that resamples labels rather than just questions, and a Holm correction over 23 comparisons.Two things came out of it. First, two of my six original benchmark vocabularies, the English key and the ordinary Russian word, turned out to be training styles for both releases, and a third, the Russian phrase, was a training style for the new release only. Half of my original benchmark was not a held-out test.Second, the effect size depended on the number of candidates, differently for different vocabularies. I had first measured jargon with five candidates and slang with eighteen, which made the slang gain look far smaller than the jargon gain. With both vocabularies in both settings:English-derived jargon, strict (no exact or prefix match to training)0.369 → 0.419 (n.s. after Holm)Department names (no exact match; 2 of 18 labels share a prefix with a training option)0.018 → 0.061, both at or below chanceOn every held-out vocabulary made of words, the new release is better in both settings, though not every gain survives the Holm correction. On abbreviations and opaque codes there is no usable gain. The two releases differ in more than the augmentation (I also fixed the split and trained four epochs instead of three), so this compares two trained models rather than a clean ablation. Two replicates of the v1.1 recipe scored 0.658 and 0.622 on jargon with five candidates, against 0.633 for the release, so small differences in the table should not be read as reproducible; the jargon gains are large relative to that spread. The contrast I almost published between jargon and slang came from comparing a five-candidate effect with an eighteen-candidate one.Accuracy and confidence also diverged. Where accuracy rose, the risk–coverage curve mostly improved, but with eighteen candidates the number of wrong answers given above 0.8 confidence went up on jargon (all labels, 79 to 109 per 1,000) and on slang, because the new release is more confident overall. On department names it went down.Seed every split from the name of the thing being split, never from a stream shared with other code.Define comparability as everything the model consumes, then compute the overlap and print it.Measure leakage directly: what fraction of the new validation set appears in the old training set.Pick a control that must not move. A fix that does not predict what stays the same is not understood.Keep one denominator per table, and replace any figure read off one random split with its distribution over splits.Verify artefacts by the content your change is supposed to alter, not by a hash against a copy of unknown age.Check every probe vocabulary against the training data before calling it held out. Test wording at more than one candidate-set size, with styles that were not in your augmentation, and resample labels, not just questions.Author’s note: The name references Jev, a commercial decision model by TypeSafe AI. Ru-Jev is an independent project, not affiliated with TypeSafe AI and not trained on Jev outputs.
